Content:
Suppose that we are given the infinite power series
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n^2}=x +\frac{x^2}{2^2}+\frac{x^3}{3^2}+\frac{x^4}{4^2} +\cdots \,.]

Content:
This series is a function of [MATH: x,] and it may converge for some values of [MATH: x] and diverge for other values. How can we determine the values of [MATH: x] for which the series is convergent?

Content:
One method that often works is the ratio test for convergence. We define [MATH: a_n=\dfrac{x^n}{n^2},] and we calculate the limit of the ratio of two successive terms, as follows:
[MATH: L|= lim_(n → ∞)|(a_{n + 1})/(a_{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)|(x^{n + 1})/((n + 1)^{2}) ⋅ (n^{2})/(x^{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)(n^{2})/((n + 1)^{2})|x|; =|x|lim_(n → ∞)(n^{2})/((n + 1)^{2}); =|x|lim_(n → ∞)(n^{2})/(n^{2} + 2n + 1); =|x|lim_(n → ∞)(1)/(1 + (2)/(n) + (1)/(n^{2})); =|x|⋅ 1; =|x|]

Content:
The ratio test says that the series converges if [MATH: L<1,] diverges if [MATH: L>1,] and is inconclusive if [MATH: L=1.] So, the series converges if [MATH: |x|<1.] Therefore, the series converges for any [MATH: x] that lies in the open interval [MATH: (-1,1).]

Content:
Unfortunately, the ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence when [MATH: |x|=1,] so the endpoints [MATH: x=1] and [MATH: x=-1] need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

Content:
- When [MATH: x=1,] we have
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n^2}= \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} = 1 +\frac{1}{2^2}+\frac{1}{3^2}+\frac{1}{4^2} +\cdots \,,]
which is convergent by the [MATH: p]-series test.
- When [MATH: x=-1,] we have
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n^2}= \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2} = -1 +\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{3^2}+\frac{1}{4^2} +\cdots]
which is convergent by the alternating series test.

Content:
Therefore, the series is convergent provided that [MATH: x \in [-1,1].] We call the interval [MATH: [-1,1]] the interval of convergence.

Content:
The radius of convergence [MATH: R] is half of the length of the interval (in the same way that the radius of a circle is equal to half the diameter of the circle). In our case, we have

Content:
[MATH: R = \dfrac{1-(-1)}{2} = 1.]

[MATH: \dfrac{|x|}{2} < 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad |x| < 2.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that we are given the infinite power series
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n^2}=x +\frac{x^2}{2^2}+\frac{x^3}{3^2}+\frac{x^4}{4^2} +\cdots \,.]

Content:
This series is a function of [MATH: x,] and it may converge for some values of [MATH: x] and diverge for other values. How can we determine the values of [MATH: x] for which the series is convergent?

Content:
One method that often works is the ratio test for convergence. We define [MATH: a_n=\dfrac{x^n}{n^2},] and we calculate the limit of the ratio of two successive terms, as follows:
[MATH: L|= lim_(n → ∞)|(a_{n + 1})/(a_{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)|(x^{n + 1})/((n + 1)^{2}) ⋅ (n^{2})/(x^{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)(n^{2})/((n + 1)^{2})|x|; =|x|lim_(n → ∞)(n^{2})/((n + 1)^{2}); =|x|lim_(n → ∞)(n^{2})/(n^{2} + 2n + 1); =|x|lim_(n → ∞)(1)/(1 + (2)/(n) + (1)/(n^{2})); =|x|⋅ 1; =|x|]

Content:
The ratio test says that the series converges if [MATH: L<1,] diverges if [MATH: L>1,] and is inconclusive if [MATH: L=1.] So, the series converges if [MATH: |x|<1.] Therefore, the series converges for any [MATH: x] that lies in the open interval [MATH: (-1,1).]

Content:
Unfortunately, the ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence when [MATH: |x|=1,] so the endpoints [MATH: x=1] and [MATH: x=-1] need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

Content:
- When [MATH: x=1,] we have
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n^2}= \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} = 1 +\frac{1}{2^2}+\frac{1}{3^2}+\frac{1}{4^2} +\cdots \,,]
which is convergent by the [MATH: p]-series test.
- When [MATH: x=-1,] we have
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n^2}= \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2} = -1 +\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{3^2}+\frac{1}{4^2} +\cdots]
which is convergent by the alternating series test.

Content:
Therefore, the series is convergent provided that [MATH: x \in [-1,1].] We call the interval [MATH: [-1,1]] the interval of convergence.

Content:
The radius of convergence [MATH: R] is half of the length of the interval (in the same way that the radius of a circle is equal to half the diameter of the circle). In our case, we have

Content:
[MATH: R = \dfrac{1-(-1)}{2} = 1.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Radius of Convergence of a Given Power Series

Example Prompt:
Find the radius of convergence [MATH: R] of the series
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n}x^n}{n \cdot 2^n} = -\frac{x}{1 \cdot 2} + \frac{x^2}{2 \cdot 2^2}-\frac{x^3}{3 \cdot 2^3}+\frac{x^4}{4 \cdot 2^4}+\cdots \,.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To apply the ratio test, we define [MATH: a_n=\dfrac{(-1)^{n}x^n}{n \cdot 2^n}.] Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as [MATH: n\to\infty\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: L|= lim_(n → ∞)|(a_{n + 1})/(a_{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)|((− 1)^{n + 1}x^{n + 1})/((n + 1) ⋅ 2^{n + 1}) ⋅ (n ⋅ 2^{n})/((− 1)^{n}x^{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)|(− nx)/(2(n + 1))|; =|− (x)/(2)|⋅ lim_(n → ∞)(n)/(n + 1); =|(x)/(2)|⋅ 1; = (|x|)/(2)]

The series converges if [MATH: L< 1.] In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied if

[MATH: \dfrac{|x|}{2} < 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad |x| < 2.]

Therefore, we conclude that the radius of convergence is [MATH: R=2.]

Item 5 — Example: Finding the Interval of Convergence of a Given Power Series

Example Prompt:
Find the interval of convergence for the series
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n}}{3^n\sqrt{n}}=\dfrac{x}{3}+\frac{x^2}{3^2\cdot \sqrt{2}}+\frac{x^3}{3^3\cdot \sqrt{3}}+\frac{x^4}{3^4\cdot 2}+\cdots \,.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To apply the ratio test, we define [MATH: a_n= \dfrac{x^{n}}{3^n\sqrt{n}}.] Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as [MATH: n\to\infty\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: L|= lim_(n → ∞)|(a_{n + 1})/(a_{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)|(x^{n + 1})/(3^{n + 1}sqrt(n + 1)) ⋅ (3^{n}sqrt(n))/(x^{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)|(sqrt(n)x)/(3sqrt(n + 1))|; = (|x|)/(3)lim_(n → ∞)((sqrt(n))/(sqrt(n + 1))); = (|x|)/(3) ⋅ 1; = (|x|)/(3)]

The series converges if [MATH: L < 1.] In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for
[MATH: \dfrac{|x|}{3}< 1]
which gives
[MATH: |x| < 3.]

So, the radius of convergence is [MATH: 3,] and the series converges for any [MATH: x] that lies in the open interval [MATH: (-3,3).]

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when [MATH: L=1.] So, when [MATH: |x|=3,] we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints [MATH: x=-3] and [MATH: x=3] need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When [MATH: x=3,] we have
[MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(x^{n})/(3^{n}sqrt(n))|= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(3^{n})/(3^{n}sqrt(n)); = ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(1)/(sqrt(n)); = 1 + (1)/(sqrt(2)) + (1)/(sqrt(3)) + (1)/(sqrt(4)) + ⋯,]
which is divergent by the [MATH: p]-series test. So the endpoint [MATH: x=3] is not included in our interval.
- When [MATH: x=-3,] we have
[MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(x^{n})/(3^{n}sqrt(n))|= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 3)^{n})/(3^{n}sqrt(n)); = ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 1)^{n})/(sqrt(n)); = − 1 + (1)/(sqrt(2)) − (1)/(sqrt(3)) + (1)/(sqrt(4)) + ⋯,]
which is convergent by the alternating series test. So the endpoint [MATH: x=-3] is included in our interval.

Therefore, the interval of convergence is [MATH: [-3,3).]
